q: Which blob type is optimized for append-only operations such as logging?
exp: Append blobs only allow adding blocks to the end, never changing existing data, which makes them ideal for logs and audit trails. Page blobs are for random read/write (disks), block blobs are for general files, and 'archive blob' isn't a blob type.

q: What is the container hierarchy in Blob storage?
exp: A storage account holds containers, and containers hold blobs. File shares (with directories) belong to Azure Files, which is a different service in the same account.

q: Which CLI command creates a container named 'images'?
opts: az storage container create --name images --account-name st1 --auth-mode login
exp: az storage container create --name images creates a blob container. --auth-mode login uses your Entra identity (you need a Storage Blob Data role) instead of the account key. az storage share create makes a file share, and az container create makes a container instance (ACI).

q: Which CLI command uploads a local file to a container?
opts: az storage blob upload --container-name images --file photo.jpg --name photo.jpg --account-name st1
exp: az storage blob upload uploads a single local file (--file) to a container (--container-name) under a blob name (--name). az storage file upload is for Azure file shares, and the other commands don't exist.

q: Apps must find blobs by key-value attributes like project=alpha across containers. Which feature?
exp: Blob index tags are key-value pairs that Azure Storage indexes, so you can search across all containers with Find Blobs by Tags (for example project = 'alpha'). Blob metadata isn't indexed or searchable, resource tags apply to Azure resources rather than individual blobs, and lifecycle rules don't search.

q: Which tier fits data accessed several times a day?
exp: The hot tier has the lowest cost per access and no minimum storage period, so it's the right choice for data read or written often. Cool, cold and archive charge more for each read and have minimum periods, which makes them expensive for busy data.

q: Backups are accessed rarely, kept at least 90 days, and must be available in milliseconds when needed. Most cost-effective online tier?
exp: Cold is an online tier, so data is available in milliseconds, but storage is cheaper than hot and cool. Its 90-day minimum fits backups kept at least 90 days. Archive is cheaper still but offline (hours to read), and hot or premium would cost more than needed.

q: How can you read an archived blob within an hour if it's smaller than 10 GB?
opts: Copy it to the archive tier
exp: Rehydrating from archive has two priorities. High priority usually completes in under an hour for blobs under 10 GB, at a higher cost. Standard priority can take up to 15 hours. Copying to archive keeps it offline, and soft delete doesn't rehydrate.

q: Which TWO methods rehydrate a blob from archive?
opts: Change its tier to hot, cool, or cold (Set Blob Tier)
Copy it to a new blob in an online tier (Copy Blob)
exp: You can rehydrate an archived blob in two ways: change its tier to hot, cool or cold with Set Blob Tier, or copy it to a new blob in an online tier with Copy Blob, which keeps the archived original. Versioning and snapshots don't bring data back online.

q: A blob was moved to cool and then deleted after 10 days. What charge applies?
opts: Early deletion charge for the remaining 20 days
exp: The cool tier has a 30-day minimum. Deleting the blob after 10 days triggers an early-deletion charge for the remaining 20 days of cool storage (prorated). There's no rehydration charge because cool is online, and 180 days is the archive minimum.

q: Can you set the archive tier on a blob in a Premium block blob account?
opts: No, premium block blob accounts don't support hot/cool/cold/archive tiering
exp: Premium block blob accounts don't support the hot, cool, cold or archive access tiers; all data sits on premium SSD storage. To archive data, copy it to a standard GPv2 account and tier it there.

q: Which redundancy setting is NOT supported for the archive tier?
exp: The archive tier is only supported for accounts using LRS, GRS or RA-GRS. Accounts using ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS can't move blobs to archive, so if you need archive, choose one of the supported redundancy options.

q: A lifecycle rule should only affect blobs in the 'logs/' folder of container 'app'. What do you set in the filter?
opts: A tag on the storage account
exp: A lifecycle rule's prefixMatch filter starts with the container name, so 'app/logs/' limits the rule to blobs in the logs folder of the app container. A blobTypes filter selects block or append blobs, not folders. Account tags and resource locks don't scope lifecycle rules.

q: A lifecycle rule should move blobs to cool if they haven't been READ for 60 days. What must be enabled?
exp: Rules based on when a blob was last read (daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan) need last access time tracking enabled on the account; otherwise Azure doesn't record reads. Rules based on last modification don't need it. Versioning, change feed and soft delete aren't involved.

q: Which lifecycle action deletes old blob versions 90 days after they become previous versions?
opts: A version action: delete with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan 90
exp: Lifecycle rules have separate action blocks for the current blob (baseBlob), snapshots and versions. To clean up old versions, add a version action: delete with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan 90, which counts from when the version became a previous version. A baseBlob action would delete current blobs instead.

q: Which blob types can lifecycle management tier between hot, cool, and archive?
opts: Block blobs only (append blobs support delete only)
exp: Lifecycle management can move block blobs between hot, cool, cold and archive, and delete them. Append blobs only support the delete action, and page blobs aren't supported at all. So tiering works on block blobs only.

q: Order the tiers a typical lifecycle policy moves aging data through, from first to last:
exp: As data ages it's accessed less, so it moves to cheaper tiers: it starts hot, moves to cool, then to archive for long-term retention, and is finally deleted when you no longer need to keep it.

q: With versioning enabled, a user overwrites a blob by mistake. How do you recover the previous content?
opts: Promote the previous version to be the current version
exp: With versioning on, every overwrite keeps the previous content as an older version. To recover, promote (restore) that previous version so it becomes the current blob again. You don't need a snapshot, and container undelete is for whole containers.

q: Versioning is enabled and a blob is deleted. What happens?
opts: The current version becomes a previous version; the data is kept until the versions are deleted
The blob and all versions are deleted
exp: With versioning on, deleting a blob doesn't destroy its data. The current version becomes a previous version, which you can restore later. The data stays until those versions are deleted, for example by a lifecycle rule.

q: What's a cost consideration of enabling blob versioning on frequently overwritten data?
opts: Each version is billed, so storage costs can grow; use lifecycle rules to delete old versions
Versions are stored in a separate account
exp: Every version is a full blob that you pay to store. If data is overwritten often, versions pile up and storage costs grow. Use a lifecycle rule to delete versions older than a certain age. Versions stay in the same account and work with tiers.

q: Someone deleted a whole container by mistake. Which feature lets you restore it?
exp: Container soft delete keeps a deleted container, and all its blobs, for the retention period so you can restore it. Blob soft delete and versioning protect individual blobs, but not the whole container being deleted.

q: What retention range can you set for blob soft delete?
exp: Blob soft delete (and container soft delete) retention can be set anywhere from 1 to 365 days. During that time a deleted blob can be undeleted; after it, the data is permanently removed. The other ranges are wrong.

q: You need to restore a set of block blobs to their state from 3 days ago after a bad batch job. Which feature?
exp: Point-in-time restore returns block blobs in a container (or the account) to their state at an earlier time, which is ideal after a bad batch job. It needs versioning, change feed and blob soft delete enabled. Share snapshots are for Azure Files, object replication copies data, and rehydration is for archive.

q: Which THREE features must be enabled before you can use point-in-time restore for block blobs?
exp: Point-in-time restore rolls block blobs back to an earlier time. It needs blob soft delete, blob versioning and change feed all enabled, because it uses the change log and the stored versions to rebuild the earlier state. Static websites and hierarchical namespace aren't required (and hierarchical namespace isn't supported).

q: Regulations require that financial records can't be modified or deleted for 7 years (WORM). Which feature?
opts: Immutable storage with a time-based retention policy
exp: Immutable storage with a time-based retention policy puts blobs into a WORM state (write once, read many): for the retention period, nobody can change or delete them, not even an administrator. Soft delete and versioning still allow deletion, and a ReadOnly resource lock protects the account's settings, not the blob data.

q: Data must be preserved indefinitely during an investigation, with no fixed end date. Which immutability policy?
exp: A legal hold makes data immutable with no end date; it stays in place until someone explicitly clears it, which suits investigations or litigation. A time-based retention policy needs a fixed period. Soft delete and lifecycle rules don't prevent deletion.

q: What does locking a time-based retention policy do?
opts: The retention interval can't be shortened and the policy can't be deleted (it can only be extended)
exp: Once a time-based retention policy is locked, it can't be removed and its retention period can't be shortened; you can only extend it. This meets regulations such as SEC 17a-4. An unlocked policy can still be changed or deleted, which is why you lock it for compliance.

q: Which protocols can Azure Files shares use?
exp: Azure Files shares are reached over SMB (Windows, macOS, Linux) or NFS (Linux, premium accounts only), and through the REST API. FTP, SFTP and iSCSI aren't Azure Files protocols.

q: Which CLI command creates a 100 GiB file share named 'docs'?
opts: az storage share-rm create --storage-account st1 --name docs --quota 100
exp: az storage share-rm create creates a file share through Azure Resource Manager, with --quota setting the size in GiB. az storage container create makes a blob container, not a file share, and the other commands don't exist.

q: Which standard file share tiers exist?
exp: Standard (HDD) file shares can be transaction optimized, hot or cool, chosen to match how often files are accessed. Premium (SSD) shares live in FileStorage accounts. Archive isn't available for file shares.

q: A standard file share must grow beyond 5 TiB. What do you enable?
exp: Standard file shares are limited to 5 TiB unless you enable large file shares on the storage account, which raises the limit to 100 TiB. Premium shares are a different account kind, and versioning or hierarchical namespace don't change share size.

q: How do you mount an Azure file share on a Windows machine?
opts: net use Z: \\st1.file.core.windows.net\docs (or New-PSDrive), using credentials over SMB 445
Map it as an iSCSI LUN
exp: On Windows you mount an Azure file share over SMB with its UNC path, for example net use Z: \\st1.file.core.windows.net\docs, or with New-PSDrive. The portal's Connect button generates the script. Azure Files isn't an iSCSI target, AzCopy can't mount shares, and FTP isn't supported.

q: Which SMB version is required to mount Azure file shares from on-premises or another region?
exp: Connections from outside the Azure region, including from on-premises, must use SMB 3.x with encryption so data is protected in transit. SMB 1.0 isn't supported, and SMB 2.x only works from inside the same region.

q: How do you protect an Azure file share from accidental deletion of the whole share?
opts: Enable soft delete for file shares
exp: File share soft delete keeps a deleted file share for the retention period, so you can undelete it. Blob and container soft delete protect Blob storage, not Azure Files.

q: What's the maximum number of share snapshots per file share?
exp: Each Azure file share can have up to 200 share snapshots. With daily snapshots, that covers more than six months; Azure Backup manages and expires them for you.

q: A user deleted a single file. Share snapshots exist. How can the user restore it themselves on Windows?
opts: Use the 'Previous Versions' tab in File Explorer
exp: Share snapshots appear in Windows File Explorer under Properties → Previous Versions, so users can open or restore an earlier copy of a file themselves. There's no need to rebuild the share or contact Microsoft.

q: Can share snapshots protect you if the whole storage account is deleted?
opts: No — snapshots live in the same account, so they're deleted with it; use a delete lock and Azure Backup
exp: Share snapshots are stored inside the same storage account as the share. If the whole account is deleted, the snapshots go with it. Protect the account with a CanNotDelete lock, and use Azure Backup (whose vault-standard tier can keep copies outside the account).

q: What must be installed on a Windows Server to sync it with Azure Files?
opts: The Azure File Sync agent, with the server registered to the Storage Sync Service
exp: Each Windows Server that syncs with Azure Files needs the Azure File Sync agent installed and must be registered with a Storage Sync Service. Only then can you add its folders as server endpoints. The MARS agent is for Azure Backup, and the Azure Monitor Agent collects telemetry.

q: Order the steps to deploy Azure File Sync:
items: Create a sync group with a cloud endpoint
Install the agent on the server and register the server
Add a server endpoint to the sync group
exp: First deploy the Storage Sync Service. Then install the agent on the server and register it with that service. Next create a sync group with the Azure file share as its cloud endpoint. Finally add the server's folder as a server endpoint. A server endpoint can only be added once the server is registered and the sync group exists.

q: How many cloud endpoints can a sync group contain?
exp: A sync group syncs exactly one Azure file share (its cloud endpoint) with one or more folders on registered servers (server endpoints). To sync another file share, create another sync group.

q: Can a single registered server have server endpoints in multiple sync groups?
opts: Yes, as long as the paths don't overlap
No, one sync group per server
exp: One registered server can belong to several sync groups, as long as each server endpoint is a different, non-overlapping path (for example D:\Finance and D:\HR). The agent only runs on Windows Server, and premium shares aren't required.

q: A branch office needs fast local access to a central Azure file share. Which solution?
opts: Azure File Sync with a server endpoint on a local Windows Server
exp: Azure File Sync installs on a Windows Server in the branch office and caches the central Azure file share locally, so users open files at LAN speed while changes sync to Azure. Object replication is for blobs, GRS copies between Azure regions, and Storage Explorer is a management tool.

q: With cloud tiering, which policy ensures that at least 20% of the local volume stays free?
exp: The volume free space policy tiers files to Azure so that at least the chosen percentage (here 20%) of the local volume stays free. A date policy tiers files that haven't been accessed in a set number of days. Retention and lifecycle policies aren't File Sync settings.

q: Which operating systems can run the Azure File Sync agent?
exp: The Azure File Sync agent runs only on supported versions of Windows Server. Linux, macOS and Windows 10/11 desktop versions can't be server endpoints, although they can still mount the Azure file share directly over SMB.

q: Answer Yes or No about Azure Files:
stmts: NFS shares can be accessed from Windows clients with SMB at the same time
Azure file shares can be mounted by Azure VMs and on-premises machines
exp: A file share uses one protocol — NFS or SMB — so an NFS share can't be accessed over SMB. Shares can be mounted by Azure VMs and on-premises machines. Share snapshots are read-only. Premium file shares use SSDs.

q: Which upload approach does AzCopy and the SDK use for large block blobs?
opts: Stage blocks in parallel (Put Block) then commit the block list (Put Block List)
One single PUT of up to 1 TB
exp: Large block blobs are uploaded as separate blocks, often in parallel (Put Block), and then committed in order with Put Block List, which creates the blob. This makes uploads faster and lets failed blocks be retried. A single PUT is only for smaller blobs, and page writes are for page blobs.

q: Which feature gives a blob a read-only, point-in-time copy that you take manually?
exp: A blob snapshot is a read-only copy of a blob at a moment in time that you create yourself when you need it. Versions are created automatically on every change. Soft delete and legal hold protect data but don't create point-in-time copies.

q: You need SFTP access to Blob storage for a partner. What must be enabled?
opts: Hierarchical namespace and SFTP support with local users
exp: SFTP for Blob storage needs hierarchical namespace (Data Lake Storage Gen2) enabled and SFTP turned on. Partners sign in as local users with a password or SSH key, and their permissions are scoped to containers. Static websites, NFS and anonymous access don't provide SFTP.

ctx: Container 'reports' in GPv2 LRS account st1: versioning on, blob soft delete 14 days, container soft delete 7 days, lifecycle: tierToArchive after 90 days since modification.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A blob deleted 10 days ago can be restored
The 'reports' container deleted 9 days ago can be restored
A 120-day-old unmodified blob can be read immediately
Overwriting a blob keeps the previous content as a version
exp: Blob soft delete keeps deleted blobs for 14 days, so a blob deleted 10 days ago can be restored. Container soft delete is only 7 days, so a container deleted 9 days ago can't. After 90 days without changes the blob is in archive and offline. Versioning keeps the previous content when a blob is overwritten.

ctx: On-premises file servers in 3 branch offices need a shared central copy of data in Azure, fast local reads, and small local disks. Users authenticate with on-premises AD.
q: Which solution fits best?
opts: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering on each branch server, syncing to one Azure file share
Three separate storage accounts with GRS
exp: Azure File Sync keeps one central Azure file share in sync with servers at each branch. Cloud tiering keeps frequently used files on small local disks and tiers the rest to Azure, so local reads stay fast. NTFS ACLs, and so on-premises AD permissions, are kept. Blob replication, separate GRS accounts and DFS-R alone can't do all of this.
